1	The present disclosure relates to cordless handheld vacuum lifters, and more particularly to a cordless handheld vacuum lifter having a grip-loss warning indicator.
2

file.content: The present disclosure relates to cordless handheld vacuum lifters, and more particularly to a cordless handheld vacuum lifter having a grip-loss warning indicator.

content.content:
1	A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is used to move glass panes, stone slabs, and similar flat panels on site by suction gripping. A suction cup is pressed against the face of the panel, air is removed from the space enclosed between the cup and the panel, and the resulting difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in that enclosed space clamps the cup to the panel so that the panel can be carried.
2	
3	A suction grip is only as good as its seal. Dust on the panel, a textured or porous surface, a nick in the sealing lip, a change in temperature, or simply the slow permeation and leakage that occurs over minutes of handling will all bleed air back into the enclosed space. As air returns, the clamping force falls. The failure is progressive and, from the point of view of the person holding the panel, silent: nothing about the feel of the tool changes until the cup lets go, at which point a heavy panel is already falling.
4	
5	Vacuum lifting equipment has therefore long been fitted with vacuum monitoring. In one known lifter for transporting loads having an adhesion surface, a suction plate assembly carries projecting annular seals defining a vacuum chamber connected to a main vacuum source, a battery-fed emergency vacuum source that can be started by an emergency switch is additionally provided, and a pressure pickup associated with the vacuum chamber is coupled with a malfunction alarm such that the alarm is turned on when a preset limit pressure is exceeded during vacuum operation [REF:US-5310232-A]. That equipment is a suction plate assembly with a main vacuum source and a separate emergency vacuum source; the alarm is described as a malfunction alarm tied to a preset limit pressure, and the reference does not describe the limit pressure in terms of the vacuum still needed to keep hold of the load.
6	
7	Control systems for vacuum lift equipment have also been described in which a programmable controller interprets feedback from vacuum level sensors and battery sensors and responsively provides warnings and limits or alters machine functions, including evaluating a change in measured vacuum level over time to determine a rate of vacuum level change that may be caused by a leak and outputting a warning indication when that rate exceeds a threshold rate [REF:US-10518985-B2]. Such a system is built around a controller with memory, stored records, and machine-function interlocks, and its leak warning is a response to how fast the vacuum is changing rather than to where the vacuum sits relative to the point at which the grip would fail.
8	
9	Powered suction devices in a hand-carried format are also known. An electric vacuum suction lifter has been described having a main body with a suction surface carrying first and second annular sealing units that bound a sealed space, a control unit, a vacuum pump controlled by the control unit to draw air from the sealed space, a pressure sensing unit that measures the pressure of the sealed space to generate instant pressure information, a battery unit that is charged by external power equipment and powers the control unit, pump, and pressure sensing unit, a start button, a pressure relief button, and at least one handle by which a member gripped by the device can be carried [REF:US-10625955-B2]. In that device the instant pressure information is compared with a high predetermined pressure and a low predetermined pressure: reaching the high predetermined pressure stops the pump, and falling below the low predetermined pressure restarts the pump. A warning unit is described as being operated when the detected battery power is below a predetermined battery power, and warning information relating to pressure is described as being transmitted to an external electronic device. A closely similar electric suction cup has likewise been described, in which the pressure detection unit detects the pressure between the suction cup and the component in real time and the vacuum pump automatically acts again when that pressure is lower than a second predetermined pressure [REF:CN-110630621-B].
10	
11	Other hand-carried powered suction devices have likewise been described. A cordless wand device for grasping objects such as silicon wafers has a housing with a hollow interior, a tip attached to the housing through a hollow tube and having a perimeter region contoured to form an airtight seal when placed against the surface of the object, a power source and a vacuum pump positioned within the housing, a switch by which the pump is turned on and off, and light-emitting diodes of different colours which indicate to an operator whether the power source is sufficiently charged to generate sufficient suction force to safely grasp the object, the sufficiency being determined from the voltage drop across a resistor network fed by the power source [REF:US-5374090-A]. What is indicated there is the state of the power source and the sufficiency of the suction force for taking hold, not how much hold remains on an object already being carried.
12	
13	A portable electric carrying suction cup structure has been described in which a handle is fixed to the upper end of a suction cup body and a vacuum pump is provided on the suction cup body, with a control unit connected between the pump and the power supply part, so that air is pumped out from between the suction cup body and the surface of a smooth material and is continuously pumped out after an airtight state has been reached in order to avoid loosening and falling during movement; the control unit is provided with a pressure gauge by which the user can know the pressure change, with a light source displaying different usage states, and with a buzzer for sending out alarm sounds according to different usage states [REF:CN-2806399-Y]. Here again the answer to a decaying grip is to keep the pump running, and what the buzzer is tied to is a usage state rather than the amount of grip left.
14	
15	A digital display suction cup has been described comprising a suction cup and a handle structure, the two ends of the handle structure carrying a switch button and a pressure relief valve, the handle structure carrying a battery and an electric vacuum pump connected to the suction cup through an air pipe, and the lower part of the battery end carrying an air pressure sensor and a display screen which displays the negative pressure value of the suction cup and the battery power, the battery being charged through a USB charging port [REF:US-2024424646-A1]. That device puts a number in front of the user and leaves the reading of the number, and the judgement of what it means for the panel in hand, to the user.
16	
17	A portable hand grab has been described including one or more suction cups, at least one handle connected to the suction cups, at least one electrical vacuum pump for at least partially evacuating a suction volume between the suction cups and the attachment surfaces, at least one vacuum sensor for detecting a vacuum level in the suction volume, a power storage unit, and an electronic controller configured to control the pump to evacuate the suction volume when the vacuum sensor detects the vacuum level being less than a preselected minimum vacuum level, together with an attach indicator which the controller activates when the vacuum sensor detects the vacuum level being greater than a preselected safe vacuum level [REF:WO-2017156581-A1]. The indicator there reports that attachment has been achieved, being activated above a preselected safe vacuum level, and the response to a vacuum level below the preselected minimum is once more to run the pump.
18	
19	A sucker for plate glass has also been described in which the sucker body defines a suction hole at its suction surface and carries a manually operated vacuum pump, a sensor communicating with the suction channel that connects the two suction holes and including a piston lever which moves in proportion to the degree of vacuum, a switch closed by the piston lever when the degree of vacuum reaches a predetermined value, a power source, and a sound generator which generates sound when the switch is closed [REF:US-5184858-A]. The pump in that sucker is worked by hand, and the sound is generated when the sensor detects a predetermined degree of vacuum, the passages of record describing that value only as a predetermined value.
20	
21	Multi-cup handling equipment has been described in which two or more vacuum modules are mounted on a mounting frame, each module having a cup, an electrically powered vacuum pump, a fluid circuit, a controller, and optionally a pressure sensor and a battery, with an interface through which a user selects an operational mode of the modules, and in which each module may include indicators that indicate a functional condition of the module visually or audibly [REF:WO-2022236379-A1].
22	
23	Two shortcomings persist for a person who is holding a panel in one hand. First, the response to a decaying grip in the known powered devices is to run the pump again: the device treats a falling vacuum as a housekeeping event to be corrected, and neither [REF:US-10625955-B2] nor [REF:CN-110630621-B] relates the low predetermined pressure at which it acts to the vacuum still needed to hold the load. If the leak is larger than the pump can make up - a torn lip, a dusty or porous panel, a cracked substrate - the pump simply runs while the grip continues to decay, and the user is told nothing until the panel is gone. Second, where a signal is given at all, it is given on a condition unrelated to the hold on the load (battery state or charge sufficiency), on a rate of change, on a usage state, on the achievement of attachment above a safe level, or at a preset or predetermined value whose relationship to the load-holding capacity of the cup is not established. None of these guarantees the one thing a person carrying a slab actually needs: notice that arrives while the cup is still holding, with grip left over to get the panel down.
24	
25	There remains a need for a self-contained, cordless, hand-held vacuum lifter that tells the user that the grip is failing at a point on the decay curve at which the grip has not yet failed.
26

1	This summary introduces a selection of concepts that are described further in the detailed description. It is not intended to identify essential features of the claimed subject matter, nor to limit the scope of the claims.
2	
3	A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is disclosed. The lifter has a rigid body comprising a handle, and a suction cup carried by the rigid body. The suction cup comprises a flexible sealing lip which is placed against a workpiece. An electric vacuum pump is disposed within the rigid body and draws air through a port so as to create a vacuum between the suction cup and the workpiece, by which vacuum the suction cup grips the workpiece and retains a load. A pressure sensor monitors the vacuum. A warning indicator is driven by the pressure sensor. A rechargeable battery powers the electric vacuum pump.
4	
5	The warning indicator activates as the vacuum is lost. It does so at a warning vacuum which the vacuum reaches, as the vacuum is lost, before the vacuum reaches a release vacuum at which the suction cup ceases to retain the load. The warning indicator therefore activates while the suction cup is still retaining the load, and there is grip in reserve at the moment the user is told.
6	
7	The warning vacuum is thus fixed by reference to the release vacuum, and not by reference to the vacuum at which a pump would be asked to run again. This is what makes the warning useful in a hand-held tool rather than merely informative. A frame-mounted or suspended lifter can respond to a failing grip by itself, by cutting in a second vacuum source or by refusing to move. A cordless handheld lifter has no such recourse: the only actuator available is the person holding the handle, and a person needs an interval in which to act. Because the warning vacuum lies on the near side of the release vacuum, that interval exists by construction rather than by luck.
8	
9	In embodiments, the warning indicator warns a user before the load can be dropped. In embodiments, the workpiece is a glass panel or a stone panel.
10	
11	A method of lifting a workpiece with such a lifter is also disclosed. This summary introduces a selection of concepts that are described further in the detailed description. It is not intended to identify essential features of the claimed subject matter, nor to limit the scope of the claims.

A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is disclosed. The lifter has a rigid body comprising a handle, and a suction cup carried by the rigid body. The suction cup comprises a flexible sealing lip which is placed against a workpiece. An electric vacuum pump is disposed within the rigid body and draws air through a port so as to create a vacuum between the suction cup and the workpiece, by which vacuum the suction cup grips the workpiece and retains a load. A pressure sensor monitors the vacuum. A warning indicator is driven by the pressure sensor. A rechargeable battery powers the electric vacuum pump.

The warning indicator activates as the vacuum is lost. It does so at a warning vacuum which the vacuum reaches, as the vacuum is lost, before the vacuum reaches a release vacuum at which the suction cup ceases to retain the load. The warning indicator therefore activates while the suction cup is still retaining the load, and there is grip in reserve at the moment the user is told.

The warning vacuum is thus fixed by reference to the release vacuum, and not by reference to the vacuum at which a pump would be asked to run again. This is what makes the warning useful in a hand-held tool rather than merely informative. A frame-mounted or suspended lifter can respond to a failing grip by itself, by cutting in a second vacuum source or by refusing to move. A cordless handheld lifter has no such recourse: the only actuator available is the person holding the handle, and a person needs an interval in which to act. Because the warning vacuum lies on the near side of the release vacuum, that interval exists by construction rather than by luck.

In embodiments, the warning indicator warns a user before the load can be dropped. In embodiments, the workpiece is a glass panel or a stone panel.

A method of lifting a workpiece with such a lifter is also disclosed. The method includes placing the flexible sealing lip against the workpiece, drawing air through the port with the electric vacuum pump to create the vacuum, carrying the load on the suction cup by the handle, monitoring the vacuum with the pressure sensor while the load is retained, and activating the warning indicator as the vacuum is lost, at the warning vacuum, that is, while the suction cup still retains the load and before the vacuum has reached the release vacuum.

1	In the following description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part hereof and in which are shown by way of illustration specific embodiments. Other embodiments may be used and structural changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like numerals refer to like parts throughout.
2	
3	FIG. 1 shows a cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 in use. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 comprises a rigid body 14 comprising a handle 16, and a suction cup 10 carried by the rigid body 14. The suction cup 10 comprises a flexible sealing lip 12. A workpiece 50, such as a glass pane or a stone slab, is gripped on its face by the suction cup 10 and is carried by the user by way of the handle 16.
4	
5	FIG. 2 is a vertical section through the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100, showing the suction cup 10, the flexible sealing lip 12, the rigid body 14, an electric vacuum pump 20, a port 22, and the workpiece 50.
6	
7	The suction cup 10 carries the flexible sealing lip 12. The flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the face of the workpiece 50 and closes the suction cup 10 against that face.
8	
9	The electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14. The electric vacuum pump 20 is configured to draw air through the port 22 so as to create a vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. The pressure of the surrounding atmosphere acting on the outside of the suction cup 10 then clamps the suction cup 10, and with it the rigid body 14 and the handle 16, to the workpiece 50, so that a load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum. Running the electric vacuum pump 20 draws further air through the port 22 and increases the vacuum; air leaking back is a loss of vacuum and a weakening of the grip.
10	
11	FIG. 3 shows the arrangement schematically. A pressure sensor 30 is configured to monitor the vacuum. A warning indicator 32 is driven by the pressure sensor 30. A rechargeable battery 40 is configured to power the electric vacuum pump 20. The electric vacuum pump 20 draws air through the port 22 from between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50.
12	
13	The warning function operates as follows. The electric vacuum pump 20 creates the vacuum, the user lifts and carries the workpiece 50, and the load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum. If the seal between the flexible sealing lip 12 and the workpiece 50 is imperfect, because of dust or grit under the lip, a textured or porous face, a damaged lip, or flexing of the workpiece 50, air bleeds back and the vacuum is progressively lost. From the point of view of the person holding the panel this loss is silent: nothing about the feel of the tool changes.
14	
15	Two vacuums are of interest during that loss. One is the release vacuum, the vacuum at which the suction cup 10 ceases to retain the load, that is, the vacuum at which the load can be dropped. The other is the warning vacuum, the vacuum at which the warning indicator 32 is driven to activate.
16	
17	The warning vacuum is fixed by reference to the release vacuum. It is the vacuum which is reached, as the vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50 is lost, before the release vacuum is reached. The warning indicator 32 accordingly activates at a moment when the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load, and the grip that remains between the warning vacuum and the release vacuum is a reserve. The warning indicator 32 is in this way configured to warn a user before the load can be dropped. During the interval that runs from the activation of the warning indicator 32 to the arrival of the vacuum at the release vacuum, the user still has a held load and a working grip. Nothing in the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 has to intervene and nothing has to be fast, because the reserve is what buys the time, and the reserve exists by construction from where the warning vacuum has been fixed.
18	
19	This is a different design decision from choosing a vacuum at which to run a pump again. A restart value is a value at which a pump is run again; it says nothing about how much grip is left, and a device that answers its crossing by running its pump will, when the leak is larger than the pump can make up, run the pump all the way past the release vacuum without ever telling the user that the grip is going. Fixing the warning vacuum by reference to the release vacuum instead is what gives the activation of the warning indicator 32 the meaning that the grip is failing and that the user still has hold of the panel. It is also a different decision from warning on how fast the vacuum is changing: a warning given on rate fires on a fast leak whatever grip is left, and stays quiet on a slow leak that has nonetheless eaten the whole reserve. And it is a different decision from reporting that attachment has been achieved, or that the battery is charged, or that a measured value can be read off a display, none of which tells a user carrying a slab how much of the hold is left.
20	
21	The distinction matters more for a hand-carried tool than for equipment on a frame or a boom. Frame-mounted and suspended lifters can be given their own remedies for a failing grip: a second vacuum source, a reservoir, an interlock that refuses further motion. A cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 has none of these. The only thing that can act on a failing grip is the person holding the handle 16, and a person needs to be told while there is still something to be done. Fixing the warning vacuum by reference to the release vacuum is what puts the warning inside the window in which the user can act.
22	
23	In embodiments, the workpiece 50 is a glass panel or a stone panel, the flexible sealing lip 12 being placed against a face of the panel. Such a panel is the workpiece 50 for which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is principally intended.
24	
25	A method of lifting a workpiece 50 with the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is shown in FIG. 4. At a placing step 202, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against a face of the workpiece 50. At an evacuating step 204, the electric vacuum pump 20, powered by the rechargeable battery 40, draws air through the port 22 and creates the vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. At a carrying step 206, the workpiece 50 is lifted and a load is carried on the suction cup 10 by the handle 16, the load being retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum.
26	
27	At a monitoring step 208, the pressure sensor 30 monitors the vacuum while the load is retained. At an activating step 210, as the vacuum is lost, the pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32 to activate at the warning vacuum, which is reached before the release vacuum at which the suction cup 10 ceases to retain the load. The warning indicator 32 is therefore activated while the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load.
28
